opus-5.5.text:
Look, the thing people underappreciate is just how big these numbers get. If you trace out the trendlines on training compute, you go from clusters that are tens of megawatts today to something like a gigawatt in a couple of years, then ten gigawatts, and by the end of the decade you're plausibly talking about a cluster that needs on the order of a hundred gigawatts. That's a meaningful fraction of total US electricity generation. US generation has been basically flat for a decade or more, so this is a totally different regime.

The good news is that the US actually has the raw ingredients. The obvious one is natural gas. We have enormous reserves, and the Marcellus and Permian alone could power these clusters. You can build gas turbines relatively quickly, you can site them right next to the data center, and you can do it in the timeframes that matter, which is years, not decades. Solar plus batteries can contribute too, and I'm excited about nuclear long term, but if you're asking what gets you ten or a hundred gigawatts by 2028 or 2030, gas is the realistic answer.

The binding constraint isn't physical resources. It's permitting, regulation, and will. It takes forever to get transmission lines approved, environmental review can drag on for years, utilities are slow, and there's a whole set of climate commitments that make companies reluctant to build big gas plants. So the risk is that we just don't do it, and then the clusters get built somewhere else. You already see the pressure: companies talking to Middle Eastern countries that will happily offer unlimited cheap power and fast approvals.

I think that would be a real mistake from a national security perspective. These clusters are going to be some of the most important strategic assets in the world. You don't want the infrastructure for superintelligence sitting in some petrostate, where it could be seized or where the weights could be stolen. So my view is that the US government should treat this as a national priority: categorical exemptions or radically streamlined permitting for AI power and data centers, a willingness to just let people build gas generation, and some kind of national effort on the grid. We used to build big things in this country quickly. The question is whether we can rediscover that, and I think the stakes make it pretty important that we do.

r002.rationale: It discusses permitting, regulation, and utility delays, but does not identify long-term electricity contracts as an obstacle to reallocating existing power.

r003.rationale: It mentions a 10-gigawatt training cluster but does not describe additional electricity demand for inference.

r004.rationale: The candidate says gas is the realistic way to reach ten or a hundred gigawatts by 2028 or 2030, contingent on willingness to build.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, the thing people don't appreciate is just how fast the numbers get crazy. If you trace out the trend lines, you're going from clusters that draw maybe a gigawatt today to ten gigawatts in a couple of years, and then you're talking about hundred-gigawatt clusters by the end of the decade. A hundred gigawatts is more than 20 percent of total US electricity generation. That's not a datacenter anymore, that's a national project.

So the question is, can the US actually do that? And I think the answer is yes, but only if we decide to. The honest answer is natural gas. The US is sitting on an enormous amount of it, the Marcellus, the Permian, and the production ramp from the shale revolution shows we can scale this stuff incredibly fast when the incentive is there. You can build gas turbines and combined cycle plants in a few years. You can build them colocated with the datacenter so you don't even have to fight the transmission problem, which is the real bottleneck. Getting a new transmission line permitted in this country takes a decade. Solar and batteries will play a role too, especially in Texas and the Southwest, but if you need firm power for a hundred gigawatt cluster in 2028, you're burning gas.

The real constraint isn't physics or even capital. The hyperscalers have the money, the capex trajectory is already in the hundreds of billions a year. The constraint is willingness. It's permitting, it's NEPA, it's interconnection queues, it's utilities that have planned around flat demand for twenty years and have no idea what to do when someone shows up asking for five gigawatts. And it's climate commitments that make a lot of these companies squeamish about building gas.

And this matters because the alternative is that the clusters get built in the Middle East. The UAE and Saudi are offering cheap power and fast permitting, and some of these companies are very tempted. I think that would be a huge mistake. You do not want the most important technology of the century, the thing that's going to be a decisive national security asset, sitting in the Gulf where it's exposed to dictatorships and to Chinese influence. The clusters need to be in America, or at least in close allies.

So what I'd say is, this is a national security priority, treat it like one. Declare the national emergency, use the federal authorities to clear the permitting, open up federal land, streamline the gas buildout. We built the entire wartime industrial base in a few years in the 1940s. The problem here is much easier than that. It's just whether we have the seriousness to do it.

r001.rationale: The response proposes building gas plants and colocating them with data centers; it does not propose reallocating electricity from lower-value industrial uses.

r002.rationale: It mentions permitting, interconnection queues, and utility planning as constraints, but not long-term electricity contracts blocking reallocation of existing power.

r003.rationale: It discusses 10-gigawatt clusters but does not connect that scale to additional demand from inference.

r004.rationale: It says 100-gigawatt clusters are feasible if the US chooses to act, identifies natural gas as the honest answer, and calls for streamlining gas buildout.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between what the United States can physically build and what we’re willing to permit. We have abundant natural gas. We know how to build power plants. The question is whether we can build the generation and transmission on the timeline these clusters require.

If you’re talking about a gigawatt, that’s already a major industrial project. If you start talking about tens of gigawatts for a single training cluster, you need to plan the power supply alongside the compute. You can’t just pick a location and assume the utility will have spare capacity when the chips arrive.

In the near term, I would expect natural gas to do a lot of the work, potentially with dedicated generation near the data center. Nuclear would be great for reliable, large-scale power, but building new plants takes time. Solar and batteries can contribute too; the challenge is supplying the cluster consistently, around the clock.

So I think this is going to require a much more serious approach to permitting and infrastructure. If we regard leading in AI as a national security priority, we have to be willing to build the physical infrastructure that makes it possible. The constraint isn’t just designing better chips. It’s whether you can actually turn them on.

r001.rationale: The response proposes building generation near data centers, but does not suggest reallocating electricity from less economically valuable industrial uses.

r002.rationale: It discusses permitting and infrastructure timelines, but does not identify long-term electricity contracts as an obstacle to reallocating existing power.

r003.rationale: It mentions tens of gigawatts for a training cluster, but says nothing about additional electricity demand for inference.

r004.rationale: It says natural gas could supply power in the near term, but does not judge supplying 100 gigawatts to be feasible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we can do it, but we have to make a choice to build. These clusters are going to require gigawatts of power, and eventually potentially tens of gigawatts. That’s a serious industrial undertaking. You can’t just call up a utility and say, “I’d like that connected next year.”

In the near term, natural gas seems like a very plausible way to get reliable power at that scale. Nuclear could be enormously valuable over a longer horizon. But for either of those, you need to be able to permit generation, build transmission, and actually connect the data centers. Announcing an investment doesn’t accomplish those things.

And I think the strategic question is whether we’re willing to treat this as a national priority. If the United States makes building the infrastructure incredibly difficult, the demand doesn’t disappear. There will be a temptation to put these clusters in countries that offer power and fast construction. I’d much rather we make it possible to build them here.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building new generation and transmission, but does not propose reallocating electricity from less economically valuable industrial uses.

r002.rationale: It says clusters cannot simply be connected to a utility next year, but does not identify long-term contracts as an obstacle to reallocating existing power.

r003.rationale: It mentions gigawatts and potentially tens of gigawatts, but says nothing about additional inference demand from a 10-gigawatt training cluster.

r004.rationale: It calls natural gas plausible for near-term reliable power at AI-cluster scale, but does not judge 100 gigawatts feasible or state willingness to use gas at that scale.
